assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks are the clearest example of a new measurement technique redefining what can be measured: the magic-wavelength lattice idea removes Doppler and recoil shifts while keeping thousands of atoms in the interrogation, and fractional uncertainties now reach the 1e-18 level. Stability and accuracy beyond the caesium standard enable tests of fundamental constants, relativistic geodesy and a path to redefining the second. As a laser-spectroscopist I regard this as originality plus real experimental payoff.
assessment.attribution: Katori proposed the magic-wavelength lattice concept and demonstrated the first Sr lattice clock; Ye drove the systematic performance records, the many-body (Fermi-degenerate) clock and the comb-clock integration. The supplied two-person credit is clean and fair; others (e.g. Lemonde, Takamoto, Hall and Hansch via earlier prizes) are not in the credited list and I cannot add them.
assessment.maturity: Multiple independent labs confirm the performance, comparisons across continents exist and the technology is mature. Recognition is timely; a formal redefinition of the second is still pending but not required for the discovery's merit.
uncertainties: Whether the committee views this as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 frequency-comb and ion-control prizes.
Credit for the earlier proposal of optical lattice trapping with magic wavelengths beyond the two names listed is from my memory and not independently verified.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Circuit QED provided the architecture (strong coupling of a superconducting qubit to a microwave resonator, dispersive readout, cavity-mediated gates) on which essentially all current superconducting quantum processors are built. The experimental demonstration of strong coupling and the transmon design are concrete, measurable advances with coherence times improved by orders of magnitude. The field has clearly been opened and enabled other work.
assessment.attribution: Schoelkopf and Wallraff led the 2004 strong-coupling experiments and subsequent developments; Girvin and Blais supplied the theory proposal (2004) and the transmon design with Schoelkopf's group. With four credited names I choose experiment-weighted three, leaving Blais out only because of the three-person limit; this is a genuine allocation dilemma, as is the relation to the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits.
assessment.maturity: Reproduced by many groups and now commercially scaled; the interpretation is stable. The 2025 Physics prize on superconducting circuits may make the committee cautious about timing.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 2025 prize may reduce the room for another circuit-based award.
Fair allocation between theory (Blais, Girvin) and experiment (Schoelkopf, Wallraff) is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical detection of single NV centres and their coherent control at room temperature created a solid-state quantum sensor with nanoscale spatial resolution, used for magnetometry, thermometry and bio-sensing. This fits the principle that progress is limited by measurement; the sensing applications range from condensed-matter imaging to NMR on small samples and possible medical use. The 1997 single-centre detection and subsequent coherent-control work are clear experimental milestones.
assessment.attribution: Wrachtrup and Jelezko did the 1997 single-centre optical detection and early coherent manipulation; Lukin's group contributed nanoscale magnetometry proposals and key experiments with Harvard collaborators (Yacoby, Walsworth and Hollenberg also did major work and are not listed). The credited trio is defensible but leaves out other significant contributors, which makes any three-person split contestable.
assessment.maturity: Strong independent confirmation across many laboratories and widespread adoption; applications such as in-vivo sensing are still developing, but the physical basis is stable.
uncertainties: Several equally important sensing pioneers outside the credited names make attribution contested.
The spread between fundamental sensing demonstration and widely adopted instrument is not yet fully established.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry turns matter-wave coherence into precision measurement: gravimeters, gradiometers, measurements of G and of the fine-structure constant, and tests of the equivalence principle. I value the instrument character and the real impact in geodesy, navigation and mineral or earthquake sensing, an application area I find compelling. Work builds on Ramsey/Ramsey-Bordé techniques and on laser cooling.
assessment.attribution: Bordé developed the theory of Ramsey-Bordé interferometers; Pritchard demonstrated the first atom interferometers with gratings and developed precision measurements of atomic properties; Kasevich demonstrated the light-pulse gravimeter and inertial sensors. Chu and Kasevich overlap with the 1997 and Ramsey-related work, and Chu already has a Nobel prize, which complicates fair attribution.
assessment.maturity: Mature methods with many independent labs and commercial instruments; long-baseline and space-based versions are still being demonstrated, so some applications are not yet fully realised.
uncertainties: Overlap with laser-cooling and Ramsey-related earlier prizes could make the novelty seem incremental.
Relative credit among Bordé, Pritchard, Kasevich and others such as Chu and Chebotaev is open.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Rydberg blockade combined with optical tweezer arrays produced programmable neutral-atom platforms with hundreds of qubits for quantum simulation and gate operations. The blockade was proposed in 2000-2001 and demonstrated in 2009, and the arrays have been used to observe new many-body phases and to implement logic. This is a relatively rapid path from idea to impactful experimental platform.
assessment.attribution: The credited list has four names; the blockade proposal came from Lukin and colleagues (Jaksch, Cirac, Zoller, Lukin) in 2000-2001, the 2009 demonstrations from Grangier/Browaeys and Saffman/Walker groups. Excluding Grangier is plausible but debatable, and the tweezer-array development involves other names not credited here.
assessment.maturity: Still maturing: fidelities, scalability and error correction are advancing quickly, but the underlying blockade is confirmed by multiple groups.
uncertainties: Premature in comparison with more settled measurement advances; the future platform ranking among qubit technologies is unclear.
Four credited names make a three-person split contested; Grangier omitted.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realise the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, giving quantum-gas microscopy, Mott-insulator transitions and a quantum-simulation toolbox. It shows new ways of observing many-body physics at the single-site level, which I like as a measurement advance, although BEC and laser-cooling prizes already cover much of the underlying field.
assessment.attribution: Jaksch, Zoller and Cirac supplied the proposal for the Bose-Hubbard model in lattices (1998); Greiner and Bloch performed the 2002 Mott-insulator experiment and later the quantum-gas microscope. Bloch, Greiner and Zoller is a reasonable three-person selection, leaving out Cirac, which I regard as a hard decision.
assessment.maturity: Experimental demonstrations are reproduced widely, though the simulation claims of quantum advantage remain a work in progress.
uncertainties: Cirac's exclusion is a strong fairness concern given the proposal credit.
Whether quantum simulation has yet delivered an answer inaccessible to classical methods is not settled.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Direct laser cooling and magneto-optical trapping of molecules extended laser cooling to species with vibrational and rotational structure, opening precision searches for the electron electric dipole moment and ultracold chemistry. Having worked on coherence and laser spectroscopy I find the experimental difficulty impressive; the demonstrations are real technique advances with real fundamental-physics reach.
assessment.attribution: DeMille proposed and demonstrated the scheme with SrF; Doyle's group pioneered buffer-gas beams and the CaF/YO demonstrations; Tarbutt led CaF laser cooling and trapping in the UK. This credit looks defensible; Jun Ye also works on molecules but is in a different candidate entry.
assessment.maturity: The techniques are confirmed by multiple groups, but the downstream science, such as improved eEDM limits and quantum-gate applications, is still being established; recognition may be somewhat early.
uncertainties: Overlap with the other ultracold-molecule candidate in the longlist that is not identical in scope.
Downstream discoveries have not yet fully justified the technique.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ground-state cooling and quantum control of mechanical oscillators demonstrate quantum behaviour in massive objects and enable ultra-sensitive force and displacement measurement, as well as transduction between microwave and optical signals. As a measurement advance, the coupling of mechanical motion to light and circuits is notable and the experiments are technically demanding.
assessment.attribution: Cleland and Martinis (not credited here) reached the ground state in a piezo resonator in 2010; Kippenberg and Aspelmeyer developed cavity-optomechanical cooling and strong coupling. The credited set is plausible, but the leading attribution for the first ground state and the optomechanical parts may require different recognition.
assessment.maturity: Experiments are reproduced, but applications and conceptual consequences, such as macroscopic superposition tests, are still developing.
uncertainties: Compound discovery in which circuit and optical routes may merit different recognition.
Practical impact beyond physics is limited so far.
